lessons.title: Balancing chemical equations
lessons.description: Use conservation of atoms to balance a chemical equation with whole-number coefficients.
lessons.content: A chemical equation represents reactants changing into products. In a closed chemical reaction, atoms are rearranged but not created or destroyed. Therefore each element must have the same number of atoms on both sides.
learning_objectives: Count atoms represented by a chemical formula.
Balance a simple equation using coefficients.
Explain why subscripts in a formula must not be changed while balancing.
prerequisites: Read element symbols and simple chemical formulae.

explanation_sections.title: Count before changing coefficients
explanation_sections.body: For H2 + O2 → H2O, the left has two hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms; the right has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. Put coefficient 2 before H2O to balance oxygen, then coefficient 2 before H2 to balance hydrogen: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O.

explanation_sections.title: Coefficients, not subscripts
explanation_sections.body: A coefficient multiplies every atom in a formula. Changing the subscript changes the identity of the substance. Check each element after balancing and reduce coefficients to the smallest whole-number ratio.

worked_examples.reasoning: Two nitrogen atoms require 2NH3. That product contains six hydrogen atoms, so 3H2 supplies six hydrogen atoms.

lessons.author: ElimuQuest Curriculum Team

questions.prompt: Why must the number of each type of atom be equal on both sides of a balanced chemical equation?
options: Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed in the reaction.
Every reaction uses the same formula.
questions.correct_answer: Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed in the reaction.
questions.explanation: Balancing expresses conservation of atoms in a chemical reaction.

questions.prompt: Which is the balanced equation for H2 + Cl2 → HCl?
questions.explanation: The product coefficient 2 gives two hydrogen and two chlorine atoms, matching the reactants.

questions.prompt: When balancing an equation, which change is permitted?
options: Change a coefficient before a formula.
Change H2O into H2O2 to fix the count.
Change a reactant into a different substance.
questions.correct_answer: Change a coefficient before a formula.
questions.explanation: Coefficients change the relative number of molecules without changing each substance's formula.

lessons.title: Acids, alkalis and neutralisation
lessons.description: Compare acidic and alkaline solutions and describe a neutralisation reaction.
lessons.content: In aqueous solution, acids provide hydrogen ions and alkalis provide hydroxide ions. When an acid reacts with an alkali, hydrogen and hydroxide ions form water; the remaining ions form a salt.
learning_objectives: Use an indicator result to classify a solution as acidic, neutral or alkaline.
Identify salt and water as products of neutralisation.
prerequisites: Recognise common element symbols and simple formulae.

explanation_sections.title: Using indicators
explanation_sections.body: Indicators change colour depending on the solution. A universal indicator gives a range of colours: red/orange indicates acidic conditions, green is around neutral, and blue/purple indicates alkaline conditions. The colour should be compared with the indicator chart.

explanation_sections.title: Neutralisation
explanation_sections.body: A general word equation is acid + alkali → salt + water. For example, hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium chloride + water. Neutralisation does not mean that every mixture has exactly pH 7; the final pH depends on amounts and concentrations.

worked_examples.prompt: Name the salt formed when hydrochloric acid reacts with potassium hydroxide.
worked_examples.reasoning: The metal in the alkali supplies potassium, and the acid supplies the chloride part of the salt; water is also formed.

lessons.author: ElimuQuest Curriculum Team

questions.prompt: Which products are formed in a typical acid–alkali neutralisation?
questions.explanation: Acid + alkali produces salt and water in a neutralisation reaction.

questions.prompt: A universal indicator turns green in a solution. What is the best interpretation?
options: The solution must be a metal.
questions.explanation: Green on the universal indicator scale is associated with a pH near neutral.

questions.prompt: Which salt forms when nitric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: Nitric acid forms nitrate salts, and sodium hydroxide supplies sodium ions.
